lessons.title: Straight-line depreciation for a partial first year
lessons.intro: Your firm buys a $1,000,000 office building and places it in service halfway through March. The building depreciates straight-line over 31.5 years with no salvage value. How much depreciation can you claim in the first calendar year, and what book value remains?

steps.explain: Open the Depreciation worksheet. The first line shows which depreciation method is active — here SL, straight-line, which is the default. We want SL, so there is nothing to change.
Scroll down to LIF, the asset's life in years, and enter 31.5. A fractional life is fine under the straight-line method.

M01 is the starting month, and it packs two facts into one number: the whole part is the calendar month (3 = March) and the decimal part is how far into that month service begins (.5 = halfway). So 3.5 means mid-March.
CST is the cost of the asset. Enter 1,000,000. Depreciation amounts are plain magnitudes, not cash flows, so there is no positive/negative sign convention to worry about in this worksheet.
SAL is the salvage value — what the asset will be worth at the end of its life. Our building has none, and SAL already reads 0, so just scroll past without typing anything.
YR is the year of the schedule you want to see. It starts at 1, which is exactly the year we want, so scroll past it too.
DEP computes by itself the moment you scroll onto it — no CPT needed. The building was in service only 9.5 of 12 months, so the full-year charge of 1,000,000 ÷ 31.5 is scaled down to 25,132.28.
RBV is the remaining book value: cost minus all depreciation taken so far. 1,000,000 − 25,132.28 leaves 974,867.72 on the books.
RDV is the remaining depreciable value: cost minus salvage minus depreciation taken. Because salvage is zero here, RDV matches RBV exactly.

lessons.answer: DEP = 25,132.28 for year 1 — a partial-year charge, because the building earned depreciation for only 9.5 of the year's 12 months. Book value at year-end is 974,867.72.

lessons.title: Stepping the schedule to year 2
lessons.intro: Same building: $1,000,000 cost, 31.5-year straight-line life, placed in service mid-March, no salvage. The worksheet shows one year at a time — this lesson builds year 1, then steps the schedule forward to read year 2, the first full year.

steps.explain: Open the Depreciation worksheet. The method line reads SL — straight-line, the default — which is what we want.
Enter the 31.5-year life into LIF.
Enter 3.5 into M01: month 3 is March, and the .5 says service starts halfway through it.
Enter the 1,000,000 cost into CST.
Scroll past SAL (salvage stays at its default of 0) and stop on YR, which reads 1 — the worksheet is set to show year 1 of the schedule.
Scroll through the three results for year 1. Each computes automatically as it appears: DEP 25,132.28, then RBV 974,867.72, and finally RDV — the 974,867.72 still left to depreciate.
One more scroll down from RDV wraps back around to YR, still showing year 1. This loop — YR, DEP, RBV, RDV, back to YR — is how you walk the whole schedule.

With YR on screen, press CPT to advance the schedule one year: YR moves from 1 to 2. (The guidebook's worked example prints 2ND SET for this step, and this calculator honors that too, but its instructions name CPT as the key that steps YR forward — so CPT is the habit to build.)
DEP recomputes for year 2. The building is now in service the entire year, so the charge is the full 1,000,000 ÷ 31.5 = 31,746.03 — larger than year 1's prorated amount.
RBV drops by another year of depreciation: 1,000,000 − 25,132.28 − 31,746.03 = 943,121.69.
RDV again equals RBV because salvage is zero. Keep repeating the loop — wrap to YR, press CPT to advance a year, scroll the three results — until RDV hits zero and the schedule is done.

lessons.answer: Year 2 DEP = 31,746.03 — the first full-year charge of 1,000,000 ÷ 31.5, since only year 1 was prorated for the mid-March start. Book value at the end of year 2 is 943,121.69.
